# `silk/i64`

<!-- Generated by silk doc-reference. Do not edit by hand. -->

Sixty-four-bit signed integers for large fixed-width values and exact integer protocols.

## When to use
Use `i64` when a stable signed 64-bit range is part of storage, interchange, or arithmetic.
Prefer `isize` only for target-sized offsets; its width changes with the compilation target.

## Details
Ordinary arithmetic, narrowing conversions, division by zero, and invalid shift counts trap.
`checked*` returns [`Option`](./option.md#declaration-) instead, `wrapping*` uses arithmetic modulo 2^64, and `saturating*`
clamps at [`MIN`](#declaration-) or [`MAX`](#declaration-). Signed right shifts preserve the sign bit.

Decimal [`parse`](#declaration-) consumes the whole input and reports syntax separately from range overflow.
Use [`Format`](./format.md#declaration-) with `Format.display` for defaults or `Format.displayWith` for explicit options.
Both operations stream through a mutable `Writer` without `Allocator`. Conversion to `f32` or
`f64` can round large integers.

## Gotchas
[`MIN`](#declaration-) has no positive i64 counterpart. Use [`wrappingNegate`](#declaration-) or [`saturatingNegate`](#declaration-) for its
negation boundary. Use [`checkedDivide`](#declaration-) when division by `-1` can receive [`MIN`](#declaration-).

## Examples
### Parse a complete signed decimal value
```silk
import silk.format { Format, ParseError }

import silk.i64

import silk.result { Result }

pub fn main() -> i32 {
  let parsed = i64.parse("-42")
  let value = move parsed
    |> Result<i64, ParseError>.unwrapOr(0)
  return i64.toI32(value + 84)
}
```

Import as `i64` with `import silk.i64`.

## `negate`

```silk
pub fn negate(value: i64) -> i64
```

Returns the arithmetic negation of `value` and traps when `value` is [`MIN`](#declaration-). Use
this function when that boundary is a program error.

<a id="declaration-"></a>

## `wrappingNegate`

```silk
pub fn wrappingNegate(value: i64) -> i64
```

Returns the arithmetic negation of `value`, wrapped to the `i64` range. [`MIN`](#declaration-)
stays [`MIN`](#declaration-). Use this function for deliberate modulo arithmetic.

<a id="declaration-"></a>

## `saturatingNegate`

```silk
pub fn saturatingNegate(value: i64) -> i64
```

Returns the arithmetic negation of `value`, clamped to the `i64` range. [`MIN`](#declaration-)
becomes [`MAX`](#declaration-). Use this function when the positive boundary is required.

## `toF32`

```silk
pub fn toF32(value: i64) -> f32
```

Converts `value` to the nearest `f32` value, with ties to even. Only magnitudes below `2^24` are
exactly representable, so a larger `i64` rounds.

<a id="declaration-"></a>

## `toF64`

```silk
pub fn toF64(value: i64) -> f64
```

Converts `value` to the nearest `f64` value, with ties to even. Only magnitudes below `2^53` are
exactly representable, so a larger `i64` rounds.

## `parse`

```silk
pub fn parse(text: string) -> Result<i64, ParseError>
```

Reads the complete text as a signed decimal `i64`.

### Details

A failure contains `silk.format.NotANumber` for empty text, a leading `+`, a non-digit, or
trailing bytes. It contains `silk.format.OutOfRange` if the number is outside the `i64` range.
